strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical characterization (Theorems 4.1-4.3, with detailed proofs in the appendix) showing that widely used test-time guidance approximations (posterior mean/DPS, Gaussian/ΠGDM, optimal control/NDTM) are structurally biased estimators of the diffused likelihood that do not converge to the true Bayesian posterior even with unlimited compute. This is a clear and previously underappreciated theoretical gap in a heavily used class of methods.

Identifies and proves a second, distinct source of bias related to naive rescaling of guidance/classifier scales (Theorem 4.3), showing that tempering must be applied inside the integral defining the diffused likelihood rather than as an exponent on the estimated likelihood -- a subtle but practically important point that also applies to classifier guidance.

Proposes two concrete consistent estimators (a reparameterization-based gradient estimator and a REINFORCE-style gradient-free estimator) that are theoretically guaranteed to converge to the true posterior as sample budget increases, and gives a clear practical discussion of their relative variance behavior with an illustrative example (Appendix C).

Strong empirical support for the central 'consistency' claim: on the Lueckmann et al. Bayesian inference benchmark, C2ST for the proposed estimators visibly improves toward the optimal value with increased compute, while competing methods plateau or worsen (Fig. 3, Table 1); comparisons include both diffusion-based and likelihood-free SBI baselines, giving a thorough evaluation.

Demonstrates that the approach scales to a realistic, high-dimensional scientific inverse problem (black hole imaging with a pretrained diffusion prior), matching/exceeding SOTA PSNR against multiple modern guidance baselines (DPS, LGD, RED-diff, PnP-DM, DAPS, DiffPIR), which strengthens the practical relevance of the theory beyond toy settings.
Honest limitations section explicitly acknowledging the added computational cost of sampling from p(x|xt), and reasonable directions (few-step diffusion models) for mitigating this.
weaknesses: The proposed estimators require drawing K samples from the diffusion posterior p(x|xt) at every guidance step (and, for black hole imaging, an additional inner sampling loop), leading to substantially higher computational cost (e.g., ~2h40 per image on an H100) than single-evaluation baselines; this practical overhead is a serious barrier for large-scale or real-time use and is only partially addressed.

The double-loop practical implementation used for the black hole imaging experiment (with M<N inner diffusion steps for tractability) is a heuristic departure from the exact estimator, and the paper does not formally characterize the residual bias introduced by this approximation, despite the paper's central claim being about eliminating bias.

The gradient-based estimator, despite being introduced as one of the two main contributions, is reported to perform poorly at scale (requires many samples, high memory) and is not actually used in the flagship high-dimensional experiment, somewhat undercutting its practical significance relative to the gradient-free variant.

The controlled benchmark tasks (Section 6.1) rely on closed-form priors with tractable noising convolutions, which, while methodologically justified for obtaining exact ground-truth diffusion posteriors, are lower-dimensional/simpler than realistic learned-prior settings; the paper only has one high-dimensional experiment (black hole imaging) to validate generalization to learned priors, and the PSNR improvement there over the strongest baseline (PnP-DM) is marginal (26.10 vs 26.07).

The variance comparison between gradient-based and gradient-free estimators (Appendix C) is based on a single simple 1D Gaussian example, providing limited insight into how the finding (gradient-free often has lower variance, contrary to typical REINFORCE-vs-reparameterization intuition) generalizes to more complex, higher-dimensional, or multimodal likelihoods.

strengths: The paper provides rigorous, clearly stated theorems (4.1–4.3) proving that the posterior-mean approximation (DPS), Gaussian posterior approximation (ΠGDM), and naive rescaling of guidance gradients for tempering are all structurally biased/inconsistent estimators of the diffused likelihood, regardless of computational budget — this is a valuable and largely novel theoretical contribution that clarifies a real gap in the guidance literature.

The tempering result (Theorem 4.3) is particularly interesting and underappreciated: it shows that simply scaling the likelihood gradient by γ (as done in essentially all practical classifier/reward-guidance implementations) does not correspond to sampling from the tempered posterior, which has implications beyond the specific estimators studied.

Two concrete, consistent estimators are proposed (reparameterization-based and REINFORCE-based), and the paper carefully analyzes their relative variance behavior (Section 5.3), offering practical guidance on when to prefer each.

The synthetic Bayesian inference benchmark (Section 6.1) is well designed: it uses tractable priors so that the true posterior and diffused likelihoods are exactly known, cleanly demonstrating that CBG's error vanishes with more compute while baselines plateau at a biased solution (Figure 3, Table 1), and it also compares against a reasonably comprehensive set of likelihood-free simulation-based inference baselines.

The black hole imaging experiment is a genuine high-dimensional test using a real pretrained diffusion prior, and the paper documents its experimental protocol, hyperparameter search, and computational cost in the appendix (facilitating reproducibility), and honestly reports the required 2h40/image cost.
The limitations section is honest about the reliance on sampling p(x|xt) being potentially expensive.
weaknesses: The consistent estimators fundamentally require sampling from the diffusion denoising posterior p(x|xt); for real pretrained diffusion models this itself must be approximated via full (or partial) reverse diffusion sampling, nested inside every guidance step. This produces an O(NM) or O(N·K) cost blow-up relative to single-pass baselines like DPS, and the paper reports 2h40 per image versus what are presumably much cheaper baselines — this substantial overhead is not clearly quantified against baselines in the main text and undermines the practical significance of the method for realistic, expensive priors.

Because of this cost, the gradient-based (reparameterization) estimator is explicitly abandoned for the high-dimensional black hole task ('we do not consider it for high-dimensional experiments'), so the paper's flagship 'scalable' result relies solely on the gradient-free/REINFORCE variant, whose own weight-degeneracy problems under sharp likelihoods are acknowledged but not fully resolved (Section 5.3).

On the more realistic black hole imaging benchmark, the reported improvement over the strongest baselines is marginal (CBG 26.10 vs. PnP-DM 26.07 vs. DPS 25.86, with std ≈ 3.7–3.9), i.e., well within one standard deviation — 'matches SOTA' is an accurate characterization but this weakens the practical case for calibrated guidance in a genuinely high-dimensional, learned-prior setting, which is precisely the regime the paper argues matters most (scientific imaging).

The synthetic benchmark tasks (Section 6.1), while cleanly illustrating the theoretical claims, use closed-form analytic priors (Gaussian/uniform) rather than learned diffusion priors, so they do not actually test the paper's central claim in the setting for which it is motivated (pretrained diffusion models as priors); the one experiment that does use a learned prior (black hole imaging) yields only marginal gains as noted above.

Baseline coverage in the empirical comparison is incomplete relative to the related work discussion: NDTM and TFG, which are discussed at length in Sections 2.3 and 3 as key comparison points for the theoretical critique, are not included as empirical baselines in Figure 3/Table 1 or Table 2.

No wall-clock or likelihood-evaluation-count comparison with baselines is presented for the black hole task in the main paper (only qualitative hyperparameter tuning ranges in the appendix), making it hard for a reader to assess the practical cost-benefit tradeoff of adopting CBG versus, e.g., PnP-DM which achieves essentially the same PSNR.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical contribution: the paper proves (Theorems 4.1–4.3, with detailed proofs in the appendix) that the three dominant families of diffused-likelihood approximations used in test-time guidance (posterior-mean/DPS-style, Gaussian/ΠGDM-style, and optimal-control/NDTM-style) are structurally biased and remain biased even with unlimited compute, and that naive rescaling of the guidance term does not implement a valid tempered posterior. This clarifies a genuine and previously under-examined gap between 'reward maximization' and 'Bayesian posterior sampling' in the guidance literature.

The proposed Calibrated Bayesian Guidance (CBG) framework is well-motivated: both the reparameterization-based estimator and the REINFORCE-based (gradient-free) estimator are derived directly from the defining integral for the diffused likelihood, are shown to be consistent (bias vanishes as K→∞), and the gradient-free variant notably supports non-differentiable rewards, broadening applicability.

Strong empirical validation on the SBI-benchmark tasks: Figure 3 and Table 1 convincingly show that CBG's C2ST score improves toward the theoretical optimum as compute increases, while baselines (DPS, LGD, DPG, SCG) plateau or even worsen — directly substantiating the paper's central inconsistency claim rather than merely asserting it.

The black-hole imaging experiment demonstrates that the approach scales to a genuine high-dimensional scientific inverse problem with a pretrained diffusion prior, achieving PSNR competitive with or exceeding strong recent baselines (DAPS, PnP-DM, DPS), and qualitative results (Fig. 4, 6, 7) support the quantitative gains.

Good analytical comparison between the gradient-based and gradient-free estimators (Section 5.3, Appendix C), offering practical guidance on when each is preferable, plus a clearly documented algorithm, extensive hyperparameter sweeps, and appendix task specifications that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Computational cost is a serious practical limitation: the consistent estimators require sampling K draws from p(x|xt) at (potentially) every diffusion timestep, and the black-hole imaging experiment already requires ~2h40 per image on an H100 GPU — this raises real concerns about scalability to larger, higher-resolution natural-image or text-to-image settings, which the paper does not test.

The Bayesian-inference benchmark experiments rely on tasks with tractable analytic priors (Gaussian/uniform) that permit exact sampling from p(x|xt), which is a favorable/idealized setting; the single high-dimensional experiment (black-hole imaging) uses a learned prior but only one dataset/domain, so the generality of the consistency benefits to typical learned diffusion priors (e.g., natural images) is not well established.

While the estimators are proven consistent asymptotically (K→∞), no finite-sample bias or variance bounds/rates are provided, so practical guarantees at the modest sample budgets used in experiments (e.g., K=512) rest only on empirical curves rather than theory.

The important theoretical result on tempered posteriors (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.2) is illustrated only qualitatively on a 1-D toy example (Figure 1, right); there is no quantitative experiment in Section 6 validating that CBG correctly samples tempered posteriors p(x|y,γ) at scale.
Several relevant recent baselines discussed in Related Work (TFG, MPGD, DCPS) are omitted from the main quantitative comparisons in Section 6, limiting how comprehensive the empirical comparison is.

The reported PSNR improvement over the strongest baseline in black-hole imaging (26.10 vs. PnP-DM's 26.07, DPS's 25.86) is marginal relative to the standard deviations reported (~3.7–3.9), so the 'matches/slightly exceeds SOTA' claim, while defensible, is not a decisive empirical win and mainly serves to show CBG is competitive rather than clearly superior on this task.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical contribution: formally proves (Theorems 4.1, 4.3, Example 4.2, with full proofs in Appendix A) that widely used guidance approximations (posterior-mean/DPS, Gaussian/ΠGDM, optimal-control/NDTM) are inconsistent estimators of the diffused likelihood, and separately proves that naive rescaling of the guidance term does not recover the correctly tempered posterior. This clarifies a subtle but important gap in the training-free guidance literature.

Proposes two theoretically consistent estimators (reparameterization-based and REINFORCE-based) that provably reduce bias as compute increases, directly addressing the identified pitfalls, and provides a practical variance analysis (Section 5.4, Appendix C-D) comparing the two.

Strong, well-designed empirical validation: a controlled 1D visualization (Figs. 1-2) intuitively illustrates the failure modes; a comprehensive Bayesian-inference benchmark (Lueckmann et al. tasks) compares against many diffusion-based and likelihood-free SBI baselines, showing CBG's C2ST score improves monotonically with compute while baselines plateau/diverge (Fig. 3, Table 1) — directly demonstrating consistency versus bias.

Practical efficiency contribution: the renoising trick with one-/few-step models reduces the O(KN^2) cost of naive posterior sampling to O(KN), enabling application to a high-dimensional scientific inverse problem (black hole imaging) where CBG sets a new SOTA PSNR and scales predictably with K (Table 2, Fig. 5, Fig. 9).

Broad applicability demonstrated beyond toy/scientific settings, with proof-of-concept extensions to natural image super-resolution and prompt-aligned text-to-image generation (Section 6.3, Appendix I), including a nontrivial tiled variant of the estimator to handle high-dimensional sparse rewards.

Honest and specific limitations discussion (measure-zero likelihood support issue) rather than generic hedging, and thorough appendices with proofs, algorithm box, hyperparameter tables, and additional ablations (bias/variance, χ² metrics) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The best empirical gains on the high-dimensional black-hole task require very large sample counts (K up to 65,536, ~6h/sample even with the fast renoise trick), which is a substantial practical cost that is somewhat downplayed relative to the framing of the method as broadly 'efficient'; the more modest K=512 setting only ties existing SOTA rather than beating it.

The renoising trick (Eq. 21) used to approximate p(x|xt) with deterministic one-/few-step models is acknowledged by the authors to be heuristic and not proven to sample the correct diffusion posterior, so the paper's consistency guarantees do not strictly transfer to the practical high-dimensional pipelines used in the main scientific/image experiments.

The core Bayesian-inference benchmark experiments use tasks with fully analytic priors/diffused posteriors (Appendix F), sidestepping the harder and more common case where p(x|xt) must itself be approximated from a learned diffusion model — this is reasonable as a controlled test of estimator bias but somewhat limits how directly the headline benchmark results generalize to realistic learned-prior settings.

The image-domain experiments (Section 6.3 and Appendix I) use a different prior model (pixel mean-flow) than the baselines they are compared against in Table 5, and require an additional non-trivial tiling scheme not discussed in the main text; this confounds direct comparison and makes the 'proof of concept' feel somewhat preliminary relative to the polished Bayesian-inference and black-hole results.

For the black-hole task, the one-step mean-flow model used for fast sampling is itself distilled from synthetic data generated by the original diffusion model, introducing an extra approximation layer whose effect on the reported consistency/accuracy claims is not separately quantified.

The impact/ethics statement is essentially boilerplate and does not engage with any specific considerations (e.g., dual-use of scientific imaging reconstruction, or trust implications of using miscalibrated posteriors in other prior applied works being critiqued).

strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-formalized theoretical account of why common test-time guidance approximations (posterior-mean/DPS, Gaussian/ΠGDM, optimal-control/NDTM) are inconsistent estimators of the diffused likelihood, with formal theorems (4.1, 4.3) and a concrete counterexample (4.2) backed by proofs in the appendix.

The identification that naively rescaling the likelihood gradient by a guidance scale γ does not correspond to sampling from the correctly tempered posterior (Theorem 4.3) is a genuinely useful and underappreciated point, connecting diffusion guidance practice to tempered/power-posterior Bayesian inference.

Two concrete consistent estimators are proposed (reparameterization-based and REINFORCE-based), each with clear derivations, and practical considerations (variance behavior, computational cost, renoising shortcuts) are discussed thoughtfully in Section 5.4 and the appendix.

The experimental section is broad: a controlled simulation-based-inference benchmark with closed-form priors/likelihoods (good for isolating estimator bias), a scientific inverse problem (black hole imaging) with a real pretrained prior, and qualitative image-domain experiments (super-resolution, prompt alignment).

Extensive ablations are provided (bias/variance decomposition in Appendix D, gradient-free vs gradient-based variance comparison in Appendix C, K-scaling curves, χ² diagnostics), which supports the internal consistency of the proposed estimators' claims within the paper's own benchmarks.
weaknesses: The central practical validation of 'calibration' (C2ST close to the optimal 0.5) is confined to low-dimensional (2-10 dim) synthetic tasks with analytic, tractable priors; the realistic high-dimensional experiments (black hole imaging, super-resolution) report only point-estimate metrics (PSNR, SSIM, FID) and never re-verify calibration/distributional fit in these settings, so the paper's headline claim of 'calibrated' inference is not actually demonstrated where it matters most.

The method's scalability is questionable: achieving competitive or superior performance in the black hole imaging task requires K up to 65,536 posterior samples per step and ~6 hours of inference per image (Table 2), while baselines complete in tens of seconds; at matched compute budgets the PSNR gains over existing methods (e.g., 26.10 vs 26.07 for PnP-DM) are marginal, undermining the practical significance of the 'new SOTA PSNR' claim.

The efficient sampling scheme relies on a heuristic 'renoising' trick with a distilled one-step/few-step model (Section 5.3) that is explicitly acknowledged as heuristic and not theoretically justified; since the consistency guarantees of the proposed estimators depend on exact samples from p(x|xt), using this approximate proxy silently reintroduces the very kind of unaccounted-for bias the paper criticizes in prior work, without a matching theoretical analysis.

For the super-resolution experiment, the method requires an additional ad hoc tiling/local-softmax decomposition of the likelihood that is not derived from, nor shown consistent with, the paper's own theoretical framework; this undisclosed additional approximation weakens the novelty-over-bias narrative built in Sections 4-5.

The core estimators (Equations 16 and 20) are explicitly noted to coincide with concurrent work (Potaptchik et al., 2026), which somewhat dilutes the claimed originality of the proposed framework, leaving the paper's main novel claims resting more on the theoretical bias analysis than on the estimators themselves.

The prompt-alignment image experiment is presented only qualitatively (Figure 6) without any quantitative metrics or baseline comparison table, which is inconsistent with the otherwise quantitative rigor of the rest of the paper and makes the claimed benefit hard to verify.

The theoretical results, while nicely formalized, largely follow from a Jensen's-inequality-type argument (mean of a nonlinear function vs. function of the mean) that is intuitive and partially anticipated by prior work cited by the authors themselves (e.g., Sun et al., 2024), somewhat limiting the conceptual novelty of the bias analysis relative to its formal presentation.

strengths: The paper provides rigorous theoretical analysis (Theorems 4.1, 4.3, Example 4.2) that clearly identifies why existing test-time guidance estimators (posterior mean, Gaussian approximation, optimal control, naive tempering) are structurally biased and inconsistent, with formal proofs in the appendix.

The proposed Calibrated Bayesian Guidance (CBG) framework is well-motivated and offers two complementary consistent estimators (gradient-based reparameterization and gradient-free REINFORCE), supporting both differentiable and non-differentiable rewards.

The efficient approximate posterior sampling via renoising with one-step/few-step models is a practical and clever solution to the computational bottleneck of naive DDPM rollouts, with empirically demonstrated near-identical performance at orders of magnitude faster inference.

Extensive empirical validation across a diverse set of tasks: a controlled Bayesian inference benchmark with closed-form posteriors (comparing against both diffusion-based and likelihood-free baselines), a challenging real scientific inverse problem (black hole imaging) achieving new SOTA PSNR, and qualitative image-domain tasks (super-resolution, prompt alignment).

Thoughtful ablations and diagnostics (bias/variance decomposition in Appendix D, variance comparison between gradient-based/free estimators in Appendix C, χ² consistency metrics, tiling strategy for high-dimensional sparse rewards) that support the paper's claims and demonstrate scientific rigor beyond just reporting final numbers.
Honest and specific limitations section acknowledging failure modes when the likelihood concentrates on a measure-zero manifold relative to the prior.
weaknesses: The core consistency guarantee relies on many samples K from p(x|xt); in high-dimensional settings (black hole imaging, super-resolution) achieving good performance requires very large K (up to 65536), with correspondingly large runtime (~6h for best result in Table 2), raising questions about practical applicability versus faster but technically biased baselines that run in seconds.

The efficient renoising trick (Eq. 21) to sample from p(x|xt) is acknowledged as heuristic/deterministic rather than a theoretically justified sample from the true stochastic posterior, which could undermine the paper's central consistency argument in the practical implementations actually used for the headline high-dimensional results.

The super-resolution experiment required an ad hoc tiling scheme to work around the sparse-reward problem, and the method still underperforms strong baselines on perceptual metrics (LPIPS, FID) in Table 5 of the appendix, suggesting the 'calibrated' approach may trade off standard task performance even in cases where distributional calibration may not be the end goal.

Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 are stated only in informal form in the main text and rely on additional regularity assumptions (Assumption A.1) not discussed in the main paper, making it harder for readers to assess the generality/tightness of the claims without consulting the appendix.

Comparisons in the Bayesian inference benchmark and black hole imaging largely use custom or lightly-tuned baseline hyperparameters; while reasonable effort appears to have been made (e.g., sweeping and using published settings), the breadth of hyperparameter sweeps for CBG vs. baselines is not perfectly symmetric, leaving some residual uncertainty about fairness of comparisons.

The claimed 'new state-of-the-art PSNR' on black hole imaging is attained only at the largest, most expensive compute budget (K=65536), which may limit the practical significance of the headline claim for time-constrained scientific pipelines.
